record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in the Theory of Computation as Questions about Two-Way Deterministic Pushdown Automaton Languages
record.original_question: Is the class 2DC of languages accepted by two-way deterministic counter machines equal to the class 2NC accepted by two-way nondeterministic counter machines?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A two-way counter machine is a finite-state device equipped with a read-only two-way input tape (with end markers) and a single counter that holds a nonnegative integer. In one step the machine reads the current input symbol and the sign-status of the counter (zero or positive), then chooses a next state, a head movement (left, stay, or right), and a counter operation (increment, decrement, or no change). The machine is deterministic if its transition function assigns at most one move to each configuration (a 2DC machine) and nondeterministic otherwise (a 2NC machine). A language is accepted by such a machine if, on input w, the machine has at least one computation that enters an accepting state.

Let 2DC denote the class of languages accepted by two-way deterministic counter machines, and 2NC the class of languages accepted by two-way nondeterministic counter machines. Decide whether
2DC = 2NC,
that is, whether every language accepted by some two-way nondeterministic counter machine is also accepted by some two-way deterministic counter machine.
artifact.status_search_result: Chrobak (MFCS 1984, "Nondeterminism is essential for two-way counter machines", LNCS 176, pp. 240–244) proved that two-way nondeterministic counter automata are strictly more powerful than two-way deterministic ones, i.e., 2DC ⊊ 2NC. Thus the equality question is settled in the negative.

status_evidence.snippet: Chrobak shows that two-way nondeterministic counter automata are strictly more powerful than deterministic ones.
